title: Klar v. H. & M. Parcel Room, Inc.
summary: The parcel-room operator could not enforce a $25 liability limitation without adequate notice and assent to that special contractual restriction.

sections.Parties: A customer left a package with a parcel-room operator and received a claim check. The person seeking return of the package sued after the operator mistakenly delivered it to someone else.
sections.Material Facts: The operator charged ten cents for checking a brown-paper package containing valuable furs. Its ticket prominently displayed the word “Contract” and purported to limit liability to $25. The customer did not read the ticket. When the package could not be recovered, its alleged contents were worth $1,000. Judges disagreed over the significance of the short printed notice, its prominent caption, the opportunity to read it, and the small checking fee.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court awarded nearly the alleged full value. The appellate court affirmed rather than reducing recovery to the ticket’s $25 limit. The casebook reports the decision and the subsequent affirmance without opinion; it supplies a shorter account rather than a full principal opinion.
sections.Issue: Did receiving the claim check amount to assent to a special limitation on the operator’s responsibility for loss, including loss caused by its negligence?
sections.Holding: The limitation was not established as part of the agreement. A ticket understood as a means of identifying the parcel did not automatically communicate the special restriction on liability.
sections.Reasoning:
The court recognized that a bailee could limit responsibility through an agreement. It required the operator to show adequate notice of the special contract and the customer’s assent. The ordinary function of this piece of paper mattered: a customer might understand it as proof of the right to collect a package rather than as a new bargain about loss.

The competing view emphasized that the word “Contract” was conspicuous, the document was brief, and the fee was trivial in relation to the asserted value. The majority nevertheless treated the transactional setting as important to whether a limitation had been communicated and accepted. The inquiry resembles Specht’s concern with whether an act performed for one apparent purpose signals assent to another set of terms.

learning.why: Klar connects the physical form of a notice with its expected function. It helps explain why the bare availability of words is different from reasonably communicating their contractual significance.

topics.assent: Receipt of a claim check did not automatically signal assent to a negligence-liability limitation.
topics.notice: The ticket’s identifying function affected what the customer reasonably understood.
topics.adhesion: The case tests a limitation in routine standardized paperwork.
